name: Primary motor cortex (M1) — toe representation
function: The most medial part of the motor strip, tucked into the paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere: it drives the intrinsic foot and toe muscles through the most medial (and longest-running) corticospinal fibres. Its medial position is why a foot-predominant weakness points at an anterior cerebral artery territory lesion rather than at the convexity, and why the foot and bladder representations are described together on the medial surface.

anchors.gyrus: paracentral lobule and the medial end of the precentral gyrus, behind the superior end of the cingulate sulcus
anchors.somatotopicOrder: order 0 of 7, arc s = 0.00 au from the toe

contextNote: Authored v9 record for the toe segment of the somatotopic map. PLACEMENT IS SCHEMATIC ON THE DERIVED ctx-hemisphere-l RIBBON, not a gyral or cytoarchitectonic boundary: the centre is the ribbon vertex nearest to an authored landmark on the precentral bank, measured with nearest-vertex projection by .dsh-scratch/somatotopy-probe7b.mjs (residual 0.04 au = 0.05 mm to the nearest surface vertex; mean triangle edge 1.31 au = 1.57 mm; 1 au = 1.2 mm). The patch reads its outward normal (-0.759, 0.633, 0.15) from that vertex and its half-sizes [3.8, 3.0, 3.0] au from the measured spacing between neighbouring segments; the ordering coordinate is the arc length along the fitted strip (s = 0.00 au at this segment), strictly increasing from toe to larynx on both strips. Why the number matters: nearest-vertex residuals came down from a first-pass min 0.56 / median 2.60 / max 3.93 au (probe4) to min 0.01 / median 0.04 / max 0.16 au on M1 and min 0.29 / median 0.78 / max 2.29 au on S1, so the two S1 segments that snap to a different fold (foot/toe 1.00 au, leg 2.29 au, larynx 2.20 au) are the least certain placements in the table. clinical.syndrome: Focal motor deficit of the toe — cortical (M1) localisation
clinical.findings: Contralateral foot/leg weakness with a relatively spared hand and face; the medial position of this segment makes an anterior cerebral artery territorial infarct the leading explanation, and the deficit may be accompanied by abulia and urinary incontinence when the adjacent SMA and anterior cingulate are involved.

clinical.findings: An irritative lesion of the toe representation produces a focal motor seizure that marches to the neighbouring segment in somatotopic order (the next more lateral body part), followed by a transient Todd paresis of the same distribution.
clinical.note: Structural/epileptic; the march follows the order in `anchors.somatotopicOrder`

name: Primary motor cortex (M1) — face representation
function: The face: lower face, lips and jaw, the second-largest representation of the strip. It sits on the lower lateral convexity, medial to the tongue and larynx segments, and it is the segment that gives the corticobulbar tract its crossed-dominance rule — the lower face receives predominantly contralateral corticobulbar input and therefore weakens after a convexity lesion, while the upper face (bilateral input) does not, which is what separates a central from a peripheral facial palsy.

name: Primary motor cortex (M1) — larynx representation
function: The larynx and pharynx — the most lateral and most inferior representation, on the opercular surface at the bottom of the strip. The patch reads its outward normal (0.577, 0.816, -0.037) from that vertex and its half-sizes [3.8, 3.0, 3.0] au from the measured spacing between neighbouring segments; the ordering coordinate is the arc length along the fitted strip (s = 64.09 au at this segment), strictly increasing from toe to larynx on both strips. Why the number matters: nearest-vertex residuals came down from a first-pass min 0.56 / median 2.60 / max 3.93 au (probe4) to min 0.01 / median 0.04 / max 0.16 au on M1 and min 0.29 / median 0.78 / max 2.29 au on S1, so the two S1 segments that snap to a different fold (foot/toe 1.00 au, leg 2.29 au, larynx 2.20 au) are the least certain placements in the table. The two strips are NOT a cytoarchitectonic segmentation (no Brodmann 4/3a/3b/1/2 map exists in this atlas) and the atlas' derived ribbon does not carry central-sulcus geometry, so the Primary somatosensory cortex (S1) attribution is a position along the fitted medial-paracentral -> lateral-opercular strip, not a sulcus traced on the mesh. Its somatotopic counterpart is ctx-m1-tongue. 3D view: postcentral patch drawn by SomatotopyOverlay when the telencephalon + context layers are on; the record owns no GLB (meshes: false), so it adds no geometry to the load budget.

afferent: Thalamocortical input from the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM), with the trigeminal component for the intraoral segments — the same body-part band of the thalamic map
Corticocortical input from the M1 counterpart (ctx-m1-tongue), from S2 and from the posterior parietal cortex
Callosal fibres from the mirror segment, densest for the axial and proximal representations
efferent: Descending corticocortical projections back onto S1 and onto area 3a/area 2 subdivisions, and onto the posterior parietal association cortex for the dorsal "where" stream
Corticostriate, corticopontine and corticothalamic feedback, and (for the face and intraoral segments) corticobulbar collaterals to the trigeminal sensory nuclei

bloodSupply: Middle cerebral artery, inferior division (opercular branches).

clinical.syndrome: Cortical (S1) sensory loss of the tongue
clinical.findings: Impaired two-point discrimination, stereognosis, graphaesthesia and texture discrimination of the tongue with relatively preserved crude touch and pinprick (the spinothalamic and lemniscal primary modalities have subcortical relays): a cortical rather than peripheral pattern, and the reason a parietal convexity lesion can be mistaken for a neuropathy.

clinical.syndrome: Thalamic pain syndrome after a lesion of the ascending relay
clinical.findings: Lesions of the VPL/VPM relay that feeds this segment (or of the thalamus itself) can be followed by Déjérine-Roussy syndrome — contralateral spontaneous pain and hyperalgesia in the same body-part band that lost discriminative sensation.
clinical.note: The cortical segment itself is not the lesion, but it is the end of the pathway whose loss is described

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Sensory Pathways and the Somatosensory System'
Kaas, 'The functional organization of somatosensory cortex in primates', Ann Anat 175:509–518 (1993)

name: Primary somatosensory cortex (S1) — larynx representation
function: The larynx and pharynx on the lowest opercular band of the postcentral gyrus. It is the smallest and least certain representation of the strip — the classical homunculus labels it as part of the face segment, and its separation here follows the standard eight-part M1 decomposition rather than a distinct anatomical boundary.

anchors.gyrus: opercular surface of the precentral gyrus, at the inferior end of the strip
anchors.somatotopicOrder: order 7 of 7, arc s = 74.57 au from the toe
